problem: Existing embodied visual navigation approaches assume the action space is identical in training and testing, which rarely holds in reality (embodied mismatch), so learned policies do not transfer to agents with a different action space.
motivation: Real deployments involve robots whose action spaces differ from the training agent's, so retraining from scratch is costly. A policy built on a robust, action-agnostic state representation could be adapted to a new action space with few samples.
key_idea: A two-stage robust adversarial learning framework: adversarial training learns a robust state feature representation, then adaptation training transfers the policy to a new action space with few samples.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations can be cited. The abstract suggests that separating a robust state representation (learned adversarially) from the action-specific policy allows quick adaptation to a new action space with fewer training samples.
method: Task definition: visual navigation subject to embodied mismatch, where the action spaces differ between training and testing
Stage 1 adversary training: an adversarial mechanism learns a robust feature representation of the state
Stage 2 adaptation training: transfers the learned policy to the new action space using fewer training samples
